title: Arterial stiffness and cardiovascular events: the Framingham Heart Study
abstract: Background: Various measures of arterial stiffness and wave reflection have been proposed as cardiovascular risk markers. Prior studies have not fully evaluated whether these tonometric measures provide incremental prognostic value beyond standard Framingham risk factors in community-dwelling adults. Methods: We evaluated 2,232 participants (mean age 63 years; 58% women) in the Framingham Offspring Study who underwent arterial tonometry. Carotid-femoral pulse wave velocity (cfPWV), central pulse pressure, forward wave amplitude, and augmentation index were measured. Multivariable Cox proportional hazards models assessed incident major adverse cardiovascular disease events (CVD: coronary heart disease, stroke, or heart failure). Results: During a median follow-up of 7.8 years, 151 participants experienced a first cardiovascular event. Higher cfPWV was associated with an increased risk of incident CVD events (adjusted hazard ratio per 1-SD increase, 1.48; 95% CI, 1.16 to 1.91; P = 0.002) after adjustment for age, sex, mean arterial pressure, total and HDL cholesterol, smoking, diabetes, and antihypertensive treatment. cfPWV also improved risk reclassification for individuals at intermediate clinical risk. Conclusions: Higher aortic stiffness assessed by carotid-femoral pulse wave velocity is independently associated with a 48% increased risk of incident cardiovascular events beyond standard risk factors in the community.

title: Prediction of cardiovascular events and all-cause mortality with arterial stiffness: a systematic review and meta-analysis
journal: Journal of the American College of Cardiology
abstract: Objectives: The purpose of this study was to calculate robust quantitative estimates of the predictive value of aortic pulse wave velocity (PWV) for future cardiovascular events and all-cause mortality. Background: Aortic stiffness has emerged as an important predictor of cardiovascular risk, but pooled quantitative effect sizes across diverse participant cohorts have not been systematically synthesized. Methods: We performed a systematic review of prospective longitudinal studies evaluating aortic PWV and clinical cardiovascular events. Relative risks (RR) and 95% confidence intervals (CI) were pooled using random-effects meta-analytic models. Results: A total of 17 studies with 15,877 participants followed for a mean of 7.7 years met inclusion criteria. The pooled RR for total cardiovascular events was 1.47 (95% CI: 1.29 to 1.66) for an increase in aortic PWV of 1 m/s, and 2.26 (95% CI: 1.89 to 2.70) for high versus low PWV tertiles. The pooled RR for all-cause mortality was 1.15 (95% CI: 1.09 to 1.21) per 1 m/s PWV elevation, and 1.90 (95% CI: 1.61 to 2.24) for high versus low stiffness. Conclusions: Aortic PWV is a strong, independent predictor of future cardiovascular events and all-cause mortality across general, hypertensive, and diabetic populations.

title: Aortic pulse wave velocity improves cardiovascular event prediction: an individual participant meta-analysis of prospective observational data from 17,635 subjects
journal: Journal of the American College of Cardiology
abstract: Objectives: The aim of this individual participant data meta-analysis was to determine whether aortic pulse wave velocity (aPWV) improves prediction of cardiovascular events beyond conventional risk factors. Background: Prior meta-analyses used published aggregate data; analyzing harmonized individual participant data allows rigorous multivariable adjustment and risk reclassification assessment across demographic subgroups. Methods: Individual participant data from 16 prospective cohorts (17,635 participants; mean age 49 ± 15 years; 53% men) were analyzed. Multivariable Cox models evaluated the association between aPWV and first-ever cardiovascular disease (CVD) events. Results: During 133,818 person-years of follow-up, 1,785 events occurred. Each 1-SD increase in log aPWV was associated with an adjusted hazard ratio for coronary heart disease of 1.23 (95% CI: 1.11 to 1.35; P < 0.001), stroke of 1.28 (95% CI: 1.16 to 1.42; P < 0.001), and composite CVD events of 1.30 (95% CI: 1.18 to 1.43; P < 0.001). Risk reclassification showed net reclassification improvement (NRI) of 13.0% in intermediate-risk individuals (P < 0.001). The predictive value of aPWV was greatest in younger participants (< 60 years). Conclusions: Aortic PWV improves prediction of major cardiovascular events, particularly in intermediate-risk individuals and younger populations.

title: Recommendations for Improving and Standardizing Vascular Research on Arterial Stiffness: A Scientific Statement From the American Heart Association
abstract: Arterial stiffness is recognized increasingly as a surrogate end point for cardiovascular disease. The American Heart Association commissioned this scientific statement to review the methodology of arterial stiffness assessment, standardize clinical terminology, provide consensus guidelines on measurement protocols, and summarize the epidemiological evidence linking arterial stiffness to cardiovascular morbidity and mortality. Carotid-femoral pulse wave velocity (cfPWV) remains the noninvasive reference standard for measuring central arterial stiffness. To ensure measurement fidelity and reproducibility across clinical trials, surface distance measurement should be standardized using 80% of the direct tape measure distance between the carotid and femoral recording sites. This scientific statement provides detailed consensus recommendations regarding pre-test preparation, environmental controls, blood pressure calibration, tonometric device certification, and clinical interpretation thresholds.

title: Aortic stiffness is an independent predictor of all-cause and cardiovascular mortality in hypertensive patients
abstract: Although various studies reported that pulse pressure, an indirect index of arterial stiffening, was an independent risk factor for mortality, a direct relationship between aortic stiffness and survival had never been demonstrated in essential hypertension. We prospectively evaluated 1,980 patients with essential hypertension (mean age 50 ± 13 years; 61% men) who had baseline carotid-femoral pulse wave velocity (cfPWV) measurements. During a mean follow-up of 112 ± 32 months (up to 16 years), 107 fatal events occurred, including 59 cardiovascular deaths. In multivariable Cox models adjusted for age, sex, mean arterial pressure, smoking, diabetes, serum cholesterol, and left ventricular hypertrophy, higher cfPWV was significantly and independently associated with all-cause mortality (adjusted odds ratio per 5 m/s increase, 1.34; 95% CI, 1.10 to 1.64; P = 0.003) and cardiovascular mortality (odds ratio per 5 m/s, 1.51; 95% CI, 1.15 to 1.98; P = 0.003). This seminal study established for the first time that central aortic stiffness is a direct, independent predictor of premature death in patients with hypertension.

threeKeyLessons: Aortic stiffness measured directly by cfPWV is an independent predictor of all-cause and cardiovascular mortality in essential hypertension.

title: In familial hypercholesterolaemia, remnant cholesterol above 1 mmol/L is associated with 50% higher risk of coronary artery disease.
abstract: AimsFamilial hypercholesterolaemia (FH) leads to lifelong elevated low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol and increased risk of coronary artery disease. We tested the hypothesis that elevated remnant cholesterol additionally increases cardiovascular risk in FH.MethodsIn the Copenhagen General Population Study (CGPS) and UK Biobank, 108,751 and 428,625 individuals were classified as with or without FH according to clinical scores and genetic mutations. In the two cohorts, 7,708 and 50,997 experienced coronary artery disease, respectively.ResultsIn CGPS and UK Biobank, remnant cholesterol ≥1 mmol/L (39 mg/dL) was observed in 12% and 11% of individuals without FH (N = 104,226 and 403,172), in 33% and 40% with Simon Broome FH (N = 3,923 and 23,860), in 44% and 78% with MEDPED FH (N = 1,005 and 2,465), in 33% and 34% with DLCN FH (N = 744 and 1,207), and in 12% and 21% of individuals with genetic FH (N = 188 and 875). Likewise in the CGPS and UK Biobank, the multivariable adjusted hazard ratios for coronary artery disease by remnant cholesterol ≥1 vs. ConclusionIn familial hypercholesterolaemia, remnant cholesterol ≥1 mmol/L (39 mg/dL) vs below is associated with ≈50% higher risk of coronary artery disease, that is, above the already high risk due to lifelong genetically elevated LDL cholesterol.

discussion.authorsInterpretation: The authors demonstrate that coronary artery disease serve as integrated bio-indices reflecting cumulative lifetime arterial wall stress and injury.
discussion.agreementWithPriorLiterature: Findings strongly align with European Society of Cardiology guidelines and the Artery Society consensus on large-artery biomechanics.
discussion.physiologicalMechanisms: Progressive elastin degradation, collagen deposition, and reduced endothelial nitric oxide bioavailability combine to reduce aortic cushioning capacity (Windkessel function), thereby increasing pulsatile load on the heart and microvasculature.
discussion.clinicalImplications: Highlights the clinical imperative of screening for subclinical vascular stiffness to initiate timely preventive interventions prior to manifest organ failure.

threeKeyLessons: Vascular stiffness is an independent marker of biological cardiovascular ageing that precedes symptomatic organ failure.
Peripheral cuff blood pressure does not fully capture central pulsatile stress delivered to the coronary, cerebral, and renal circulations.
Early intervention targeting arterial compliance is essential for preventing long-term cardiovascular sequelae.

title: Severe mental illness: cardiovascular risk assessment and management.
abstract: Patients with severe mental illness (SMI) including schizophrenia and bipolar disorder die on average 15-20 years earlier than the general population often due to sudden death that, in most cases, is caused by cardiovascular disease. This state-of-the-art review aims to address the complex association between SMI and cardiovascular risk, explore disparities in cardiovascular care pathways, describe how to adequately predict cardiovascular outcomes, and propose targeted interventions to improve cardiovascular health in patients with SMI. These patients have an adverse cardiovascular risk factor profile due to an interplay between biological factors such as chronic inflammation, patient factors such as excessive smoking, and healthcare system factors such as stigma and discrimination. Several disparities in cardiovascular care pathways have been demonstrated in patients with SMI, resulting in a 47% lower likelihood of undergoing invasive coronary procedures and substantially lower rates of prescribed standard secondary prevention medications compared with the general population. Although early cardiovascular risk prediction is important, conventional risk prediction models do not accurately predict long-term cardiovascular outcomes as cardiovascular disease and mortality are only partly driven by traditional risk factors in this patient group. As such, SMI-specific risk prediction models and clinical tools such as the electrocardiogram and echocardiogram are necessary when assessing and managing cardiovascular risk associated with SMI. In conclusion, there is a necessity for differentiated cardiovascular care in patients with SMI. By addressing factors involved in the excess cardiovascular risk, reconsidering risk stratification approaches, and implementing multidisciplinary care models, clinicians can take steps towards improving cardiovascular health and long-term outcomes in patients with SMI.
